title: Where $100 of Amazon Sales Actually Goes
footnote: Illustrative model · typical third-party apparel seller · per $100 of sales · Sources: Marketplace Pulse; Amazon 2026 fee schedule

steps.label: Customer Sales
steps.sub: $100 of sales. Who actually keeps it?
steps.cue: Every time you spend one hundred dollars
steps.narration: Every time you spend one hundred dollars with a seller on Amazon... about fifty-two of those dollars never reach the seller. Not the brand. Not the factory. Amazon. And according to the U.S. government, you're paying for it too — even if you never shop on Amazon. In 2025, one line in Amazon's annual report — advertising — brought in sixty-eight point six billion dollars. That's one hundred and eighty-eight million dollars... every single day. So let's follow one hundred dollars. Dollar by dollar. Through every fee, every auction, and every return... and find out who actually gets your money.

steps.label: Product & Freight
steps.sub: Manufacturing, ocean freight and import duties — paid months before anything sells.
steps.cue: Meet a typical clothing seller on Amazon.
steps.narration: Meet a typical clothing seller on Amazon. For every hundred dollars in sales, here's where the money goes. First, the product itself. Manufacturing, ocean freight, and import duties. Twenty-eight dollars — paid months before anything sells.

steps.label: Referral Fee (17%)
steps.sub: Amazon's first cut: a 17% referral fee on apparel over $20.
steps.cue: The moment a customer clicks "Buy Now"...
steps.narration: The moment a customer clicks "Buy Now"... Amazon takes its first cut. A seventeen percent referral fee on clothing. Seventeen dollars.

steps.label: FBA, Storage & Surcharges
steps.sub: Picking, packing, shipping, storage — plus a 3.5% surcharge since April 2026.
steps.cue: Next, Fulfillment by Amazon. Picking, packing, shipping,
steps.narration: Next, Fulfillment by Amazon. Picking, packing, shipping, storage... plus a new surcharge added in 2026. About twenty dollars.

steps.label: Sponsored Ads
steps.sub: The line shoppers never see: about $15 of every $100 goes to sponsored listings.
steps.cue: Then, the line shoppers never see. Advertising.
steps.narration: Then, the line shoppers never see. Advertising. Just to show up where buyers look, a typical seller spends around fifteen dollars on sponsored listings.

steps.label: Returns & Write-offs
steps.sub: Refunds, return fees and inventory that can't be resold.
steps.cue: Returns and write-offs take another ten.
steps.narration: Returns and write-offs take another ten.

steps.label: Seller Keeps
steps.sub: The seller keeps $10. Amazon collects $52 — more than five times as much.

boxes.title: Seller keeps
boxes.sub: after product, fees, ads and returns

steps.cue: The final split? The seller — who
steps.narration: The final split? The seller — who designed the product, paid the factory, and carried all the risk — keeps about ten dollars. Amazon — without owning a single thread — collects about fifty-two. More than five times what the seller keeps. But hold on to that fifteen-dollar ad line. That's where this story gets strange.
